chapters.title: Wax, money and what it teaches

segments.text: Welcome to the show, today we talk about keeping bees on a city roof.
The first colony I ever bought arrived in a cardboard box that hummed.
Most people assume the hard part is the stings, and it is not.
The hard part is deciding when to leave the hive alone.
In my second winter I lost three hives in a single week.
Nobody tells you that a quiet hive in January can still be alive.
You put your ear against the wood and you listen for a low steady hum.
That hum is forty thousand bees shivering to keep the queen warm.
I paid two hundred dollars for a queen who died in nine days.
The supplier refunded me and told me it happens one time in twenty.
So the next spring I split my strongest colony into two.
It felt reckless, like cutting a company in half on purpose.
But the numbers say a split colony swarms far less often.
A swarm is the whole hive deciding to leave without asking you.
I watched one go over the neighbour's fence at noon on a Tuesday.
Honey is the least interesting thing a hive makes.
Wax is what actually pays, and almost nobody sells it well.
I rendered my first block of wax in a slow cooker I ruined forever.
The smell lasted a week and my landlord asked me to explain.
There is one rule I wish I had followed from the start.
Never open a hive on a cold, windy afternoon.
The bees are not angry at you, they are angry at the weather.
My friend ignored that rule and spent a night at the clinic.
He is fine now, and he still keeps bees, which tells you something.
Let me say something about money, because people always ask.
A rooftop hive costs about three hundred dollars to start.
It returns maybe forty jars in a good year, and a good year is rare.
You do this because you like it, not because it adds up.
The most surprising thing was how much the bees taught me about patience.
You cannot hurry a colony, and you cannot argue with one.
Last month a stranger knocked on my door to thank me for the lavender.
Apparently every bee on the block had been visiting her balcony.
That is the kind of payoff no spreadsheet will ever show you.
If you want to start, begin in early spring with one hive only.
Find a mentor, because a forum cannot hold the frame for you.
Thanks for listening, and thanks to the three of you still here.
